title: My Daily Brief
overview: This edition is dominated by Donald Trump's Asia trip, which culminates in a first-ever three-way meeting with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen. Democrats are consolidating power after their midterm wins: Mary Peltola flipped Alaska's Senate seat and House Democrats nominated Hakeem Jeffries for speaker. Also covered: Nvidia's board rejecting Jensen Huang's offer to return, US officials saying a string of tech outages are unrelated, South Korea's measures against AI cheating, and local Charlotte news on Duke Energy rates and a homicide.

stories.headline: Trump to meet Xi and Putin together in Shenzhen, plus a separate one-on-one with Putin
stories.summary: President Trump arrived in Shenzhen, China, for the APEC summit. On Thursday he is due to hold the first three-way talks between the leaders of the US, China and Russia. A US official said Trump will also meet Putin one-on-one, their first talks since Alaska last year. The Kremlin said the trilateral meeting will last no more than an hour and that no 'full-scale' Trump-Putin negotiations are planned. Trump says he wants to discuss denuclearization and ending the war in Ukraine, but White House officials played down expectations and analysts do not expect substantive breakthroughs.
key_facts: The trilateral meeting is scheduled for Thursday on the sidelines of APEC in Shenzhen.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said 'no more than an hour' has been set aside for the three-way meeting.
Trump and Putin shook hands for the first time in more than a year ahead of the summit.
Trump envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are meeting Ukrainian and European officials in Berlin on Thursday.
Xi and Putin condemned US sanctions on their countries, and Xi said Beijing would cut tariffs.

perspectives.framing: A Guardian editorial called the meeting historic but 'not progress', arguing that spectacle is the substance and that Xi and Putin gain stature from it. It raised concerns for Ukraine, Taiwan and US allies, and noted Trump's domestic troubles, including the midterm losses and the tech outages. AP coverage carried by PBS was more straightforward. It reported the added Putin meeting, Trump's claim that a Ukraine deal is 'very close', and the outages back home.

Centrist outlets stuck mainly to logistics and expectations: meeting times, Kremlin statements, and the Berlin talks on Ukraine. DW explained why China rejects nuclear limits and suggested 'risk reduction' steps as more realistic outcomes. The Hill highlighted Xi and Putin condemning US sanctions.

Fox News offered little coverage: a reader-reaction prompt and a short segment with a retired officer. Both framed the meeting as unprecedented and pointed to the Iran war and Ukraine as central topics.

disputed: Whether Ukraine is on the agenda: Trump's aides said before the trip it would not be, but Trump says a deal is 'very close'.
The exact timing of the Trump-Putin bilateral and what it will cover.
Whether Trump will raise Nvidia and suspected Chinese espionage; the Guardian expects he will not.
stories.why: A meeting of the three largest nuclear powers could shape the Ukraine war, arms control and US-China trade, even if expectations are low.

stories.headline: House Democrats nominate Hakeem Jeffries for speaker; 11 vote no
stories.summary: In a closed-door secret ballot on Wednesday, House Democrats nominated Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York to be speaker in the next Congress. He received 251 votes. The full House votes on January 3, and given the Democratic majority of at least 257 seats, his election is widely expected. He would be the first Black speaker. Seven incoming progressive members said in a joint statement that they voted no because talks over their priorities, including Medicare for All, immigration enforcement and Gaza, are still ongoing.
key_facts: Jeffries received 251 votes; 11 members voted against him.
The full House votes on January 3, 2027, and 218 votes are needed to win.
Katherine Clark is set to be majority leader, Pete Aguilar majority whip, and Ted Lieu caucus chair.
Republicans chose Jim Jordan as House minority leader.

perspectives.framing: The Guardian and NPR stressed the historic nature of the nomination and the size of the majority. They gave substantial space to progressives' concerns, including an Indivisible poll showing 28% favorability for Jeffries and his recent moves on Medicare and Israel. NPR quoted Jeffries on cost of living and 'unprecedented corruption'.
DW, Axios and The Hill focused on the tally, the path to January 3, and the rest of the leadership lineup, with the progressive dissent as a secondary point.

The Washington Examiner centred on the 11 dissenters. It named them, noted that five are Democratic Socialists of America members, and quoted Rep. Henry Cuellar calling them 'a small group that have marginalized themselves'. It also noted the dissenters lack the numbers to block Jeffries.

disputed: The total ballots cast differs: DW reports 265, while The Guardian and Axios report 262.
Four of the 11 'no' votes are unidentified; the Washington Examiner says Rep.-elect Don Leonard also opposed Jeffries.
According to the Examiner, Frederick Haynes signed the dissent statement but missed the vote due to illness.
stories.why: The incoming speaker will control which bills reach the House floor and steer oversight of the Trump administration for the final two years of his term.

stories.headline: Democrat Mary Peltola wins Alaska Senate race, giving Democrats a 56-44 majority
stories.summary: The Associated Press declared Democrat Mary Peltola the winner over two-term Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan after she crossed 50% of first-choice votes, so no ranked-choice tabulation was needed. It was the last Senate race to be called and the ninth Republican-held seat Democrats flipped, the most in a midterm since 1958. The final weeks were shaped by a New York Times report alleging that Peltola aides helped recruit a second candidate named Dan J. Sullivan to draw votes from the incumbent. Peltola and the other Sullivan both deny it. The Sullivan campaign did not respond to requests for comment.
key_facts: Peltola received 144,302 votes to Sullivan's 131,844, about 50.1%.
Candidate Dan J. Sullivan received 4,760 votes, fewer than Peltola's margin.
Democrats will hold a 56-44 Senate majority after flipping nine seats.
Trump won Alaska by about 13 points in 2024.
A federal judge dismissed a Justice Department bid to block certification of the results.

perspectives.framing: NPR and PBS (AP) presented the win as a political comeback in a Trump state, quoting Peltola on cost-of-living struggles. They mentioned the vote-siphoning allegations along with Peltola's denial and Trump's call for her prosecution.

Axios emphasized history: the first Alaska Native senator, powered by Alaska Native communities. DW and The Hill focused on the vote count and the size of the Democratic wave. DW noted that the margin exceeded the second Sullivan's vote total.

The Daily Caller acknowledged that Peltola won by more than the second Sullivan's vote total. Most of its article, however, detailed the alleged recruitment scheme, the DOJ's subpoenas, and the judge who blocked the lawsuit, whom it described as Obama-appointed.

disputed: Whether Peltola's campaign or the DSCC recruited the second Sullivan is alleged but denied, and the DOJ investigation is ongoing.
The reported margin varies slightly: about 12,500 by DW's figures versus 'about 13,000' per the Daily Caller.
stories.why: The result completes a large Democratic Senate majority and keeps a contested election-integrity dispute alive.

stories.headline: Nvidia board rules out Jensen Huang's return as company posts strong earnings
stories.summary: Nvidia's new chair, Harvey Jones, said the board unanimously accepted co-founder Jensen Huang's resignation and does not intend to reinstate him. Huang had offered to return earlier that day. The board said Huang resigned after disclosing personal behavior inconsistent with its code of conduct; news reports have linked him to a woman described as an alleged Chinese spy. Interim CEO Colette Kress reported revenue of about $115.8 billion, beating estimates, and raised the company's outlook. Bill Ackman, Elon Musk and a petition with about 200,000 signatures have called for Huang's return. The board says it will search for a permanent CEO without rushing.
key_facts: Quarterly revenue was $115.8 billion, more than double a year earlier; estimates were about $109.1 billion.
Nvidia projects about $130 billion next quarter and raised its fiscal 2028 growth outlook to 75%.
Shares rose almost 5% after hours but are down 24% this month.
Huang said: 'I own my mistakes completely.'

perspectives.framing: CNBC and TechCrunch emphasized business continuity and Kress's reassurances, quoting analysts who said demand 'did not leave with him'. TechCrunch also quoted Sam Altman's praise for Huang. The BBC examined Nvidia's importance to the US economy and the risks of 'circular financing'. The Hill reported the board's rejection straightforwardly.

Fox Business led with Kress's confident 'We've got this' and the earnings beats. The New York Post featured Bill Ackman's attack on the board as having 'panicked due to headlines', along with support for Huang from Musk and the petition.

disputed: The alleged link between Huang and a Chinese intelligence recruit is reported but unverified.
Ackman argues the board breached its duties; the board says Huang resigned voluntarily.
It is unclear whether Huang's exit will change Nvidia's spending and investment strategy.
stories.why: Nvidia is central to the AI boom and the US stock market, so leadership turmoil there could ripple through the wider economy.

stories.headline: Rubio says there is 'zero evidence' a week of US tech outages is linked
stories.summary: Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the US is 'not under systemic attack'. He said there is no evidence that recent outages are connected or caused by hostile actors. The outages hit Microsoft, the FAA's national flight system, JPMorgan Chase, United Airlines, Apple, and an NSA internal network. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton attributed the disruptions to system upgrades and security patches that did not go as planned. Every affected company or agency said the cause was not a cyberattack. Some experts point to a common pressure: rapid patching driven by AI-discovered vulnerabilities.
key_facts: An FAA ground stop halted US flights for more than four hours, the longest since 9/11.
Rubio said: 'We are not under systemic attack.'
Researchers at Calif reported a Java flaw found using AI; a UCL professor said it affects only a specific code library, not every Java program.

perspectives.framing: The Guardian carried Rubio's denial but added context on a newly found Java vulnerability. It quoted an expert who said AI-driven upgrades and patching are straining 'brittle' infrastructure.
The BBC and The Hill centred on Rubio's and Clayton's statements. The BBC quoted cybersecurity experts saying there is 'no conspiracy' and listed each outage with its stated cause.
The Daily Caller relayed Rubio's quotes directly, framing them as ruling out coordinated outages, with little added context.

disputed: Public fears that the outages are linked persist online; officials and experts say there is no evidence for a link.
Whether AI-driven vulnerability discovery is an underlying common cause is one expert's view, not an established finding.
stories.why: Outages hitting flights, banks and government networks affect daily life and raise questions about how resilient critical infrastructure is.

stories.headline: Trump announces Philippines trade deal and defense cooperation; Manila does not confirm a deal
stories.summary: On a state visit to Manila, Trump told President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. that the US is expanding defense cooperation, citing more than $5 billion in approved arms sales. He also floated cooperation on civilian nuclear power and an Alaska gas project. Trump said the two countries had 'consummated a very big trade deal'. The Philippine president's office referred only to an 'understanding' on economic cooperation, and its ambassador said nothing was signed. Trump also met Imelda Marcos, whom he called a longtime friend.
key_facts: Trump cited more than $5 billion in approved US arms sales to the Philippines.
Philippine Ambassador Jose Manuel Romualdez said 'None' when asked whether anything was signed.
Trump said he is 'not concerned at all' about the South China Sea.

perspectives.framing: Al Jazeera focused on Trump's reunion with Imelda Marcos, recounting her late husband's dictatorship, her lavish lifestyle and the corruption charges against her. It also quoted Trump's remark that Marcos Jr. had 'good genetics'.
CNA focused on the defense, energy and trade announcements and highlighted the gap between Trump's trade-deal claim and Manila's account. The Hill covered the Imelda Marcos visit.
The New York Post highlighted a light moment in which Trump joked about firing Rubio, prompting laughter from Rubio and Marcos.

disputed: Whether a trade deal actually exists: Trump says yes, while Philippine officials describe only an understanding and say nothing was signed.
stories.why: The Philippines is a key treaty ally amid South China Sea tensions, and the substance of the trade claims is uncertain.

stories.headline: NC regulators approve smaller Duke Energy rate hike and new rules for data centers
stories.summary: The North Carolina Utilities Commission approved Duke Energy rate increases taking effect January 1, 2027, smaller than the utility first requested. The commission also created special rates and conditions for data centers using more than 50 megawatts. These include minimum contract lengths and early-exit fees meant to keep construction costs from shifting to other customers. Advocates called the data-center rules a step in the right direction but said fuel costs and pollution remain unaddressed. Regulators also did not renew a $42 monthly bill credit for more than 87,000 low-income customers.
key_facts: Rates rise starting January 1, 2027, with a second step in 2028.
Duke says a typical Duke Energy Carolinas bill rises $9.62 per month in 2027 and another $5.89 in 2028.
The Customer Assistance Program, worth $42 per month, will not be renewed.
Duke first requested the increases in November 2025.

perspectives.framing: WFAE emphasized the impact on vulnerable customers from the end of the assistance credit, quoting an environmental lawyer on 'life or death choices'. It also detailed how the data-center tariff differs from Duke's proposal.

WSOC and WBTV focused on bill impacts and on the hike being smaller than requested. WSOC quoted an energy advocate on the remaining fuel-cost risk, and WBTV quoted Duke's statement on growth and reliability.

disputed: Reported percentages differ. WSOC says 9.5% over two years for residential customers; WFAE says 5.9% in 2027 plus 3.6% in 2028 for Duke Energy Carolinas; WBTV, citing Duke, says 4.8% residential over two years.
stories.why: Most Charlotte-area households will pay more for electricity, and the data-center rules set a precedent for who bears the cost of the AI-driven power demand.

stories.headline: South Korea tightens security for national college exam after AI cheating case
stories.summary: More than half a million people sit South Korea's suneung university entrance exam on Thursday. It follows the top scorer on this year's tax accountant exam admitting he used a concealed camera and generative AI to cheat. Prime Minister Han Seong-sook called AI-assisted cheating a 'social evil'. She ordered checks of candidates' glasses, watches and clothing, emergency phone alerts, and wifi shutdowns near exam centres, and police raised their alert level. K-pop stars sent their customary encouragement, and Ateez's San spoke out against AI cheating.
key_facts: The exam takes place at 1,312 centres on Thursday.
The tax exam cheat surrendered to police on Sunday; no charges have been filed yet.
Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin ruled out postponing the exam and said newer smart glasses cannot be perfectly screened.

perspectives.framing: The Guardian detailed the cheating scandal, the government's countermeasures, and the national effort that surrounds the exam.
Yonhap reported police security measures in an official tone. The Korea Herald framed the story through K-pop stars' encouragement messages and San's comments on cheating.

disputed: Whether others were involved in the tax exam cheating is under police investigation.
Officials acknowledge newer smart devices may evade detection.
stories.why: The case shows how generative AI and tiny cameras are challenging high-stakes testing everywhere.

stories.headline: Two separate court stories: South Korea finalizes ex-spy chief's sentence; US op-ed defends the Supreme Court
stories.summary: These two articles are unrelated. In South Korea, the Supreme Court upheld a 2.5-year prison sentence for former intelligence chief Cho Tae-yong. He was convicted of falsely claiming that former President Yoon Suk Yeol did not order arrests of politicians during the 2024 martial law, along with false testimony and deleting call records. In the US, a Reason post highlighted Professor William Baude's New York Times op-ed. Baude argues that the Supreme Court has ruled against the Trump administration in major cases and that partisan court reform, now being discussed after the Democratic sweep, would be dangerous.
key_facts: Cho was acquitted of dereliction of duty at all court levels.
Baude cites rulings against the administration on the National Guard, emergency tariffs, birthright citizenship and Federal Reserve independence.

perspectives.framing: Yonhap gave a straight legal account of the Korean ruling and its charges.
Reason's Volokh Conspiracy endorsed Baude's defense of the US Court and his warning against partisan reform. It called the focus on judicial ethics 'superficial' and one-sided.

disputed: Whether the Democratic Congress will pursue Supreme Court reform or expansion is a matter of debate, not yet action.
stories.why: Both stories concern how courts hold executive power to account, in Korea after martial law and in the US amid calls for court reform.

stories.headline: Police investigate homicide at east Charlotte park
stories.summary: Charlotte-Mecklenburg Police are investigating a homicide reported around 11:45 a.m. Wednesday in the 1300 block of Tarrington Avenue in east Charlotte, near East Independence Boulevard. Police have not said how the person died, how many people were involved, or whether anyone was arrested. A park entrance was cordoned off, and police were expected to give an update in the afternoon.
key_facts: The homicide was reported around 11:45 a.m. on November 18 on Tarrington Avenue.
No arrests or details about the victim have been released.

perspectives.framing: All three local TV stations gave brief, developing-news accounts. WSOC added neighbors' concern about violence near a park used by families.

disputed: The exact location differs: WSOC says Sheffield Neighborhood Park, WCNC says Evergreen Nature Preserve, and the reported cross streets differ (Leeds Drive vs. Pierson Drive).
stories.why: Local residents may want to know about a violent incident in a public park while details are still emerging.
